All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. Cycles are considered as subgraphs, not necessarily induced subgraphs. A graph homomorphism from \(G\) to \(H\) is a map \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(f(u)f(v)\in E(H)\) whenever \(uv\in E(G)\); the map need not be injective.

For a real number \(c\in[0,1]\), consider the following property: there exists a finite graph \(H_c\) containing no cycle of length \(3\) such that, for every integer \(n\geq1\), every graph \(G\) on \(n\) vertices containing no cycle of length \(3\) or \(5\), and in which every vertex has at least \(cn\) neighbors, admits a homomorphism to \(H_c\). The graph \(H_c\) may depend on \(c\), but not on \(n\) or \(G\).

What is the exact infimum of the numbers \(c\in[0,1]\) having this property?
</problem>

A complete answer to this problem: A complete answer must give a single exact real number equal to the infimum of all c in [0,1] satisfying the stated finite triangle-free homomorphism-target property, with a proof that it is the infimum. It need not determine whether the property holds at the infimum itself.

1	# agent_1: last reply
2	
3	The exact infimum is
4	\[
5	\boxed{\frac19}.
6	\]
7	
8	I will prove both statements needed for this:
9	
10	* for every \(c>1/9\), the required finite triangle-free target exists;
11	* for every \(c<1/9\), no finite triangle-free target works.
12	
13	The proof below is self-contained, including the regularity ingredient. The Python at the end performs actual finite constructions and exhaustive checks of the relevant identities and lemmas.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## 1. Turning the problem into a coloring problem
18	
19	For a triangle-free graph \(G\), define \(J(G)\) on \(V(G)\) by joining distinct vertices whenever there is a walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) between them in \(G\).
20	
21	We need the following equivalence.
22	
23	### Lemma 1
24	A class \(\mathcal C\) of triangle-free graphs admits a common finite triangle-free homomorphic target if and only if
25	\[
26	\sup_{G\in\mathcal C}\chi(J(G))<\infty.
27	\]
28	
29	### Proof
30	
31	If \(f:G\to H\) and \(H\) is triangle-free, then \(f\), regarded as a coloring by the vertices of \(H\), properly colors \(J(G)\). Indeed, identically mapped endpoints of a three-edge walk would give a closed three-edge walk in \(H\), hence a triangle.
32	
33	Conversely, define a finite graph \(U_t\) whose vertices are
34	\[
35	(a,S),\qquad a\in[t],\quad S\subseteq[t]\setminus\{a\},
36	\]
37	with
38	\[
39	(a,S)(b,T)\in E(U_t)
40	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
41	a\in T,\ b\in S,\ S\cap T=\varnothing.
42	\]
43	This graph is triangle-free: in a purported triangle, the first coordinate of one vertex belongs to both sets associated with the other two vertices, although those sets must be disjoint.
44	
45	Given a proper \(t\)-coloring \(q\) of \(J(G)\), put
46	\[
47	S_v=\{q(w):w\in N_G(v)\},\qquad f(v)=(q(v),S_v).
48	\]
49	For an edge \(uv\), the cross-membership conditions hold. Moreover, \(S_u\cap S_v=\varnothing\), since a common color would appear at the ends of a three-edge walk through \(uv\). Thus \(f:G\to U_t\). ∎
50	
51	We shall repeatedly use another elementary observation:
52	
53	> A graph containing neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\) has no odd closed walk of length at most \(5\).
54	
55	Indeed, a shortest odd closed subwalk is an odd cycle.
56	
57	---
58	
59	# 2. Upper bound: every \(c>1/9\) works
60	
61	Fix \(c>1/9\). Choose
62	\[
63	0<\rho<\frac{c-1/9}{2},
64	\qquad D=c-2\rho>\frac19.
65	\]
66	
67	We first obtain a bounded collection of neighborhood types.
68	
69	## 2.1. Regularity preparation
70	
71	Set
72	\[
73	\alpha=\rho,\qquad d=\frac{\rho}{10},
74	\qquad \varepsilon=\left(\frac{\rho}{100}\right)^2.
75	\]
76	Choose an integer \(k_0\ge 10/\rho\).
77	
78	The equitable regularity lemma, proved in Section 4 below, gives a bounded partition
79	\[
80	V(G)=W_0\sqcup W_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup W_r,
81	\]
82	where \(|W_0|\le\varepsilon n\), all other parts have the same size \(m\), \(r\ge k_0\), and at most \(\varepsilon r^2\) pairs are not \(\varepsilon\)-regular.
83	
84	Delete every cluster incident with more than \(\sqrt\varepsilon r\) irregular pairs. There are at most \(2\sqrt\varepsilon r\) such clusters. Add them to the exceptional set.
85	
86	Write the remaining clusters as \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\), and the enlarged exceptional set as \(V_0\). Define \(R\) on \([k]\) by
87	\[
88	ij\in E(R)
89	\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
90	(V_i,V_j)\text{ is }\varepsilon\text{-regular of density at least }d.
91	\]
92	
93	Then
94	\[
95	|V_0|\le(\varepsilon+2\sqrt\varepsilon)n<\rho n. \tag{1}
96	\]
97	
98	Also, averaging the degrees of vertices in a remaining cluster \(V_i\), the possible contributions from its own cluster, \(V_0\), irregular pairs, and regular pairs of density less than \(d\), give
99	\[
100	m\,d_R(i)
101	\ge
102	\left(c-\frac1{k_0}-\varepsilon-3\sqrt\varepsilon-d\right)n
103	\ge(c-\rho)n
104	\ge Dn. \tag{2}
105	\]
106	In particular, \(R\) has no isolated vertex.
107	
108	For each \(v\in V(G)\), define
109	\[
110	S_v=\{i:|N_G(v)\cap V_i|\ge\alpha m\}.
111	\]
112	For \(S\subseteq[k]\), let
113	\[
114	U(S)=\bigcup_{i\in S}V_i.
115	\]
116	By (1),
117	\[
118	|N_G(v)\cap U(S_v)|
119	\ge cn-|V_0|-\alpha n
120	\ge Dn. \tag{3}
121	\]
122	Thus every \(S_v\) is nonempty.
123	
124	There are boundedly many possible sets \(S_v\). Call these the **types**, and denote their nonempty vertex classes by \(X,Y,Z,\ldots\). The set associated with a type \(X\) is denoted \(S_X\).
125	
126	All statements below hold once \(n\) is sufficiently large in terms of \(c\). The finitely many smaller orders will be absorbed at the end.
127	
128	## 2.2. Three consequences of excluding \(C_3,C_5\)
129	
130	The following regular-pair facts justify all the short-path embeddings we use.
131	
132	* Between two subsets of size at least \(\alpha m\) in a regular pair of density at least \(d\), there is an edge.
133	* If \(ij,j\ell\in E(R)\), subsets of size at least \(\alpha m\) in \(V_i,V_\ell\) can be joined by a two-edge path through \(V_j\).
134	
135	For the second fact, all but at most \(2\varepsilon m\) vertices of \(V_j\) have neighbors in both subsets. These statements remain true after excluding any three prescribed vertices, provided \(m\) is sufficiently large.
136	
137	They imply:
138	
139	**(A)** Each \(S_v\) is independent in \(R\).
140	
141	Otherwise, two neighbors of \(v\) in an appropriate regular pair form a triangle with \(v\).
142	
143	**(B)** If \(vw\in E(G)\), then
144	\[
145	N_R(S_v)\cap N_R(S_w)=\varnothing,
146	\qquad S_v\cap S_w=\varnothing. \tag{4}
147	\]
148	A common member of the first two sets gives a four-edge path from \(v\) to \(w\), which together with \(vw\) is a \(C_5\). The second conclusion follows from the first because \(R\) has no isolated vertices.
149	
150	**(C)** If distinct \(v,w\) have a common neighbor in \(G\), there is no \(R\)-edge between \(S_v\) and \(S_w\).
151	
152	Such an edge gives a three-edge path from \(v\) to \(w\) through two clusters. Together with their common neighbor, this is a \(C_5\).
153	
154	In particular, every type class is independent in \(G\), by (4).
155	
156	## 2.3. Small types are independent in \(J(G)\)
157	
158	Call a type \(X\) **small** if
159	\[
160	|U(S_X)|<2Dn,
161	\]
162	and **large** otherwise.
163	
164	If \(v,w\in X\) and \(X\) is small, (3) implies that \(v,w\) have a common neighbor in \(U(S_X)\). They cannot also be adjacent in \(J(G)\): the common neighbor and a walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) would give an odd closed walk of length \(3\) or \(5\).
165	
166	Consequently,
167	\[
168	\chi(J(G)[X])=1\qquad\text{for every small type }X. \tag{5}
169	\]
170	
171	## 2.4. Auxiliary graphs on a type
172	
173	Fix three types \(X,Y,Z\). Define \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) on \(X\) by joining \(x,x'\) if there is a path
174	\[
175	x-y-z-x',\qquad y\in Y,\ z\in Z,
176	\]
177	in either orientation.
178	
179	We first observe that
180	\[
181	\chi(F_{X;Y,Z})
182	\le 2^{\chi(J(G)[Y])},
183	\qquad
184	\chi(F_{X;Y,Z})
185	\le 2^{\chi(J(G)[Z])}. \tag{6}
186	\]
187	
188	For example, properly color \(J(G)[Y]\) with \(r\) colors, and color \(x\in X\) by the set of colors appearing on \(N_G(x)\cap Y\).
189	
190	For a witness \(x-y-z-x'\), the color of \(y\) appears in the set for \(x\), but not that for \(x'\). Otherwise some \(y'\in N_G(x')\cap Y\) has the same color as \(y\), although
191	\[
192	y-z-x'-y'
193	\]
194	is a three-edge walk. Thus these sets properly color \(F_{X;Y,Z}\), proving the first inequality; the other is symmetric.
195	
196	In particular, if \(Y\) or \(Z\) is small, \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) is bipartite.
197	
198	The crucial assertion is that it is also bipartite when all three types are large.
199	
200	### Claim
201	If \(X,Y,Z\) are large, then \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) is bipartite.
202	
203	### Proof
204	
205	Suppose it contains an odd cycle. Orient each edge of this cycle according to a chosen witness
206	\[
207	x-y-z-x',
208	\]
209	from its endpoint adjacent to \(Y\) to its endpoint adjacent to \(Z\).
210	
211	An odd cycle cannot have every vertex a source or a sink: these would alternate. Therefore some vertex of \(X\) has both a neighbor in \(Y\) and a neighbor in \(Z\).
212	
213	A witness also supplies a two-edge path between types \(X,Z\) and one between types \(Y,X\). Hence every pair among \(X,Y,Z\) has representatives with a common neighbor. By (A) and (C),
214	\[
215	S_X\cup S_Y\cup S_Z
216	\quad\text{is independent in }R. \tag{7}
217	\]
218	
219	The witness has edges between every pair of these types. By (B), the three sets
220	\[
221	S_X,S_Y,S_Z
222	\]
223	are pairwise disjoint, as are
224	\[
225	N_R(S_X),N_R(S_Y),N_R(S_Z).
226	\]
227	By (7), none of the first three sets intersects any of the last three.
228	
229	Each of the first three corresponding cluster unions has size at least \(2Dn\), since the types are large. Each of the last three has size at least \(Dn\), by (2) and the fact that every \(S_X\) is nonempty.
230	
231	These six disjoint unions therefore contain at least
232	\[
233	3(2Dn)+3(Dn)=9Dn>n
234	\]
235	vertices, a contradiction. ∎
236	
237	## 2.5. Bounded coloring, hence a finite target
238	
239	Let \(L\) be the number of types. It is bounded in terms of \(c\).
240	
241	For a large type \(X\), every graph \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) is bipartite:
242	
243	* if \(Y\) or \(Z\) is small, use (5)–(6);
244	* otherwise use the claim.
245	
246	Since \(X\) is independent in \(G\), every edge of \(J(G)[X]\) has a three-edge witness. Therefore
247	\[
248	J(G)[X]=\bigcup_{Y,Z}F_{X;Y,Z}.
249	\]
250	Coloring a union of graphs by the tuple of their colors gives
251	\[
252	\chi(J(G)[X])\le 2^{L^2}.
253	\]
254	The same bound holds for small types by (5). Using disjoint palettes,
255	\[
256	\chi(J(G))\le L\,2^{L^2}. \tag{8}
257	\]
258	
259	Both the number of clusters and the lower threshold on \(n\) depend only on \(c\). Thus (8), enlarged to cover smaller graphs, gives a constant \(t=t(c)\) with
260	\[
261	\chi(J(G))\le t.
262	\]
263	Lemma 1 supplies the required finite triangle-free target \(U_t\).
264	
265	This proves that every \(c>1/9\) has the property.
266	
267	---
268	
269	# 3. Lower bound: no \(c<1/9\) works
270	
271	We give an explicit finite construction.
272	
273	## 3.1. Shift graphs of arbitrarily large chromatic number
274	
275	Let \(S(m,k)\) have as vertices the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([m]\), with edges
276	\[
277	(a_1,\ldots,a_k)(a_2,\ldots,a_{k+1})
278	\qquad(a_1<\cdots<a_{k+1}).
279	\]
280	
281	For each fixed \(k\), these graphs have unbounded chromatic number as \(m\to\infty\).
282	
283	Here is an elementary proof. Given an \(r\)-coloring of \(S(m,k)\), color a \((k-1)\)-tuple \(A\) by the set of colors of its extensions to the right.
284	
285	For adjacent \((k-1)\)-tuples
286	\[
287	A=(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1}),\qquad
288	B=(a_2,\ldots,a_k),
289	\]
290	the color of \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) belongs to the set for \(A\), but not that for \(B\). Thus
291	\[
292	\chi(S(m,k-1))\le 2^{\chi(S(m,k))}.
293	\]
294	Since \(S(m,1)=K_m\), iteration proves the assertion.
295	
296	## 3.2. Many subsets independent against odd three-edge walks
297	
298	Fix an even integer \(k\ge4\). For
299	\(\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_m)\in\{-1,1\}^m\), define
300	\[
301	h_\epsilon(a_1,\ldots,a_k)
302	=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^j\epsilon_{a_j}.
303	\]
304	
305	For adjacent vertices \(u,v\) of \(S(m,k)\), cancellation gives
306	\[
307	|h_\epsilon(u)+h_\epsilon(v)|\le2. \tag{9}
308	\]
309	Consequently, for any three-edge walk \(u_0u_1u_2u_3\),
310	\[
311	|h_\epsilon(u_0)+h_\epsilon(u_3)|\le6, \tag{10}
312	\]
313	by adding the first and third edge sums and subtracting the second.
314	
315	Thus the set
316	\[
317	I_\epsilon=\{v:h_\epsilon(v)>3\}
318	\]
319	contains no two endpoints of a three-edge walk.
320	
321	For every fixed vertex, the proportion of sign vectors for which it belongs to \(I_\epsilon\) is
322	\[
323	p_k
324	=\frac12-\frac{\binom{k}{k/2}}{2^{k+1}}
325	       -\frac{\binom{k}{k/2+1}}{2^k},
326	\qquad p_k\longrightarrow\frac12. \tag{11}
327	\]
328	For completeness, writing \(k=2r\),
329	\[
330	\frac{\binom{2r}{r}}{4^r}
331	=\prod_{j=1}^r\left(1-\frac1{2j}\right)
332	\le (r+1)^{-1/2}\longrightarrow0,
333	\]
334	and the other binomial coefficient in (11) is smaller.
335	
336	## 3.3. The graph obstructing small triangle-free targets
337	
338	Fix \(c<1/9\) and a finite triangle-free graph \(H\).
339	
340	Choose even \(k\) so large that, writing \(p=p_k\),
341	\[
342	\frac{p}{3(1+p)}>c. \tag{12}
343	\]
344	Choose \(m\) with
345	\[
346	\chi(F)>|V(H)|,\qquad F=S(m,k).
347	\]
348	
349	Replace every edge \(uv\) of \(F\) by a path
350	\[
351	x_u-y_{uv}-z_{uv}-x_v,
352	\]
353	choosing an arbitrary orientation \(u\to v\) for each edge. Call the resulting graph \(Q\), with its three independent classes \(Q_0,Q_1,Q_2\) of original, first internal, and second internal vertices.
354	
355	Define a homomorphism \(\ell:Q\to F\) by
356	\[
357	\ell(x_u)=u,\qquad \ell(y_{uv})=v,\qquad \ell(z_{uv})=u.
358	\]
359	
360	Choose a positive integer \(M\), and put \(N=M2^m\). For each \(i=0,1,2\):
361	
362	* add an independent set \(U_i\), consisting of \(M\) copies of every sign vector \(\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^m\);
363	* add an independent set \(V_i\) of size \(pN\);
364	* join \(U_i\) completely to \(V_i\);
365	* join \(q\in Q_i\) to the copies of \(\epsilon\) precisely when
366	  \[
367	  h_\epsilon(\ell(q))>3.
368	  \]
369	
370	There are no other edges. Since \(m\ge k\), \(pN\) is an integer.
371	
372	Call the graph \(G\). Every vertex of \(Q\) gets exactly \(pN\) neighbors in its corresponding \(U_i\). Every vertex of \(U_i\) has \(pN\) neighbors in \(V_i\), and every vertex of \(V_i\) has \(N\) neighbors. Hence
373	\[
374	\delta(G)\ge pN,\qquad
375	|V(G)|=|V(Q)|+3(1+p)N. \tag{13}
376	\]
377	By (12), sufficiently large \(M\) makes
378	\[
379	\delta(G)\ge c|V(G)|.
380	\]
381	
382	### There are no triangles or five-cycles
383	
384	The graph \(Q\) itself has no cycle of length less than \(9\).
385	
386	A triangle or five-cycle cannot contain a vertex of \(V_i\). For a five-cycle through such a vertex, the remaining three-edge path between its two neighbors in \(U_i\) would require an edge inside \(Q_i\cup V_i\), but this set is independent.
387	
388	Now consider a short odd cycle avoiding all \(V_i\).
389	
390	* A triangle using \(U_i\) would require an edge within \(Q_i\).
391	* A five-cycle using exactly one vertex of some \(U_i\) gives a three-edge path in \(Q\) between two of its neighbors. Applying \(\ell\) and (10), their scores cannot both exceed \(3\).
392	* A five-cycle using two vertices from the \(U_i\)'s has the form
393	  \[
394	  u-q-u'-q'-q''-u.
395	  \]
396	  The common neighbor \(q\) forces \(u,u'\) to belong to the same \(U_i\). Then \(q',q''\in Q_i\), contradicting their adjacency.
397	
398	Thus \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).
399	
400	### There is no homomorphism \(G\to H\)
401	
402	Suppose \(f:G\to H\). For each edge \(uv\in E(F)\), its replacing three-edge path in \(Q\) shows that
403	\[
404	f(x_u)\ne f(x_v),
405	\]
406	because otherwise its image is a closed three-edge walk in the triangle-free graph \(H\).
407	
408	Therefore \(u\mapsto f(x_u)\) is a proper coloring of \(F\) with at most \(|V(H)|\) colors, contradicting the choice of \(F\).
409	
410	This constructs, for every finite triangle-free \(H\), a counterexample of minimum-degree ratio at least \(c\). Hence no \(c<1/9\) has the required property.
411	
412	---
413	
414	# 4. Proof of the regularity ingredient
415	
416	Here are the details needed to make the upper bound independent of an unproved regularity theorem.
417	
418	For disjoint nonempty sets \(A,B\), write
419	\[
420	d(A,B)=\frac{e(A,B)}{|A||B|}.
421	\]
422	The pair is \(\varepsilon\)-regular if every \(A'\subseteq A,B'\subseteq B\) with
423	\[
424	|A'|\ge\varepsilon|A|,\qquad |B'|\ge\varepsilon|B|
425	\]
426	satisfies
427	\[
428	|d(A',B')-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon.
429	\]
430	
431	We prove that, for fixed \(\varepsilon>0,k_0\), sufficiently large graphs have an equitable partition into boundedly many clusters, an exceptional set of size at most \(\varepsilon n\), and at most \(\varepsilon k^2\) irregular cluster pairs.
432	
433	For a partition \(\mathcal P\), define its energy by
434	\[
435	\mathcal E(\mathcal P)
436	=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{A,B\in\mathcal P}|A||B|d(A,B)^2,
437	\]
438	using ordered adjacency densities also when \(A=B\). It lies in \([0,1]\), and refinement cannot decrease it, by the weighted mean-square inequality.
439	
440	Start with \(k_0\) equal clusters and fewer than \(k_0\) exceptional vertices, treating exceptional vertices as singleton parts for energy calculations.
441	
442	Suppose there are more than \(\varepsilon k^2\) irregular pairs among equal clusters of size \(m\). Choose a witnessing rectangle for each irregular pair and refine every cluster by all its witnessing subsets. There are at most \(2^k\) resulting cells per cluster.
443	
444	For each irregular ordered block, the energy increases by at least
445	\[
446	\frac{m^2}{n^2}\varepsilon^4:
447	\]
448	the witness has relative area at least \(\varepsilon^2\), and its density differs by more than \(\varepsilon\). Accounting for both orders, the total increase exceeds
449	\[
450	2\varepsilon^5\left(\frac{km}{n}\right)^2.
451	\]
452	While the exceptional set has size at most \(n/2\), this is at least \(\varepsilon^5/2\).
453	
454	It remains to keep the clusters equal without losing control of the exception. Put
455	\[
456	s=\left\lceil4\varepsilon^{-5}\right\rceil,\qquad
457	B(k)=\left\lceil\frac{4s\,2^k}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil.
458	\]
459	After the witness refinement, subdivide every cell into pieces of common size
460	\[
461	q=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{B(k)}\right\rfloor

278	If \(v,w\in X\) and \(X\) is small, (3) implies that \(v,w\) have a common neighbor in \(U(S_X)\). They cannot also be adjacent in \(J(G)\): the common neighbor and a walk of length \(1\) or \(3\) would give an odd closed walk of length \(3\) or \(5\).
279	
280	Consequently,
281	\[
282	\chi(J(G)[X])=1\qquad\text{for every small type }X. \tag{5}
283	\]
284	
285	## 2.4. Auxiliary graphs on a type
286	
287	Fix three types \(X,Y,Z\). Define \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) on \(X\) by joining \(x,x'\) if there is a path
288	\[
289	x-y-z-x',\qquad y\in Y,\ z\in Z,
290	\]
291	in either orientation.
292	
293	We first observe that
294	\[
295	\chi(F_{X;Y,Z})
296	\le 2^{\chi(J(G)[Y])},
297	\qquad
298	\chi(F_{X;Y,Z})
299	\le 2^{\chi(J(G)[Z])}. \tag{6}
300	\]
301	
302	For example, properly color \(J(G)[Y]\) with \(r\) colors, and color \(x\in X\) by the set of colors appearing on \(N_G(x)\cap Y\).
303	
304	For a witness \(x-y-z-x'\), the color of \(y\) appears in the set for \(x\), but not that for \(x'\). Otherwise some \(y'\in N_G(x')\cap Y\) has the same color as \(y\), although
305	\[
306	y-z-x'-y'
307	\]
308	is a three-edge walk. Thus these sets properly color \(F_{X;Y,Z}\), proving the first inequality; the other is symmetric.
309	
310	In particular, if \(Y\) or \(Z\) is small, \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) is bipartite.
311	
312	The crucial assertion is that it is also bipartite when all three types are large.
313	
314	### Claim
315	If \(X,Y,Z\) are large, then \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) is bipartite.
316	
317	### Proof
318	
319	Suppose it contains an odd cycle. Orient each edge of this cycle according to a chosen witness
320	\[
321	x-y-z-x',
322	\]
323	from its endpoint adjacent to \(Y\) to its endpoint adjacent to \(Z\).
324	
325	An odd cycle cannot have every vertex a source or a sink: these would alternate. Therefore some vertex of \(X\) has both a neighbor in \(Y\) and a neighbor in \(Z\).
326	
327	A witness also supplies a two-edge path between types \(X,Z\) and one between types \(Y,X\). Hence every pair among \(X,Y,Z\) has representatives with a common neighbor. By (A) and (C),
328	\[
329	S_X\cup S_Y\cup S_Z
330	\quad\text{is independent in }R. \tag{7}
331	\]
332	
333	The witness has edges between every pair of these types. By (B), the three sets
334	\[
335	S_X,S_Y,S_Z
336	\]
337	are pairwise disjoint, as are
338	\[
339	N_R(S_X),N_R(S_Y),N_R(S_Z).
340	\]
341	By (7), none of the first three sets intersects any of the last three.
342	
343	Each of the first three corresponding cluster unions has size at least \(2Dn\), since the types are large. Each of the last three has size at least \(Dn\), by (2) and the fact that every \(S_X\) is nonempty.
344	
345	These six disjoint unions therefore contain at least
346	\[
347	3(2Dn)+3(Dn)=9Dn>n
348	\]
349	vertices, a contradiction. ∎

351	## 2.5. Bounded coloring, hence a finite target
352	
353	Let \(L\) be the number of types. It is bounded in terms of \(c\).
354	
355	For a large type \(X\), every graph \(F_{X;Y,Z}\) is bipartite:
356	
357	* if \(Y\) or \(Z\) is small, use (5)–(6);
358	* otherwise use the claim.

360	Since \(X\) is independent in \(G\), every edge of \(J(G)[X]\) has a three-edge witness. Therefore
361	\[
362	J(G)[X]=\bigcup_{Y,Z}F_{X;Y,Z}.
363	\]
364	Coloring a union of graphs by the tuple of their colors gives
365	\[
366	\chi(J(G)[X])\le 2^{L^2}.
367	\]

369	\[
370	\chi(J(G))\le L\,2^{L^2}. \tag{8}
371	\]

373	Both the number of clusters and the lower threshold on \(n\) depend only on \(c\). Thus (8), enlarged to cover smaller graphs, gives a constant \(t=t(c)\) with
374	\[
375	\chi(J(G))\le t.
376	\]

383	# 3. Lower bound: no \(c<1/9\) works
384	
385	We give an explicit finite construction.
386	
387	## 3.1. Shift graphs of arbitrarily large chromatic number
388	
389	Let \(S(m,k)\) have as vertices the increasing \(k\)-tuples from \([m]\), with edges
390	\[
391	(a_1,\ldots,a_k)(a_2,\ldots,a_{k+1})
392	\qquad(a_1<\cdots<a_{k+1}).
393	\]
394	
395	For each fixed \(k\), these graphs have unbounded chromatic number as \(m\to\infty\).
396	
397	Here is an elementary proof. Given an \(r\)-coloring of \(S(m,k)\), color a \((k-1)\)-tuple \(A\) by the set of colors of its extensions to the right.
398	
399	For adjacent \((k-1)\)-tuples
400	\[
401	A=(a_1,\ldots,a_{k-1}),\qquad
402	B=(a_2,\ldots,a_k),
403	\]
404	the color of \((a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) belongs to the set for \(A\), but not that for \(B\). Thus
405	\[
406	\chi(S(m,k-1))\le 2^{\chi(S(m,k))}.
407	\]
408	Since \(S(m,1)=K_m\), iteration proves the assertion.
409	
410	## 3.2. Many subsets independent against odd three-edge walks
411	
412	Fix an even integer \(k\ge4\). For
413	\(\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_m)\in\{-1,1\}^m\), define
414	\[
415	h_\epsilon(a_1,\ldots,a_k)
416	=\sum_{j=1}^k(-1)^j\epsilon_{a_j}.
417	\]
418	
419	For adjacent vertices \(u,v\) of \(S(m,k)\), cancellation gives
420	\[
421	|h_\epsilon(u)+h_\epsilon(v)|\le2. \tag{9}
422	\]
423	Consequently, for any three-edge walk \(u_0u_1u_2u_3\),
424	\[
425	|h_\epsilon(u_0)+h_\epsilon(u_3)|\le6, \tag{10}
426	\]
427	by adding the first and third edge sums and subtracting the second.
428	
429	Thus the set
430	\[
431	I_\epsilon=\{v:h_\epsilon(v)>3\}
432	\]
433	contains no two endpoints of a three-edge walk.
434	
435	For every fixed vertex, the proportion of sign vectors for which it belongs to \(I_\epsilon\) is
436	\[
437	p_k
438	=\frac12-\frac{\binom{k}{k/2}}{2^{k+1}}
439	       -\frac{\binom{k}{k/2+1}}{2^k},
440	\qquad p_k\longrightarrow\frac12. \tag{11}
441	\]
442	For completeness, writing \(k=2r\),
443	\[
444	\frac{\binom{2r}{r}}{4^r}
445	=\prod_{j=1}^r\left(1-\frac1{2j}\right)
446	\le (r+1)^{-1/2}\longrightarrow0,
447	\]
448	and the other binomial coefficient in (11) is smaller.
449	
450	## 3.3. The graph obstructing small triangle-free targets
451	
452	Fix \(c<1/9\) and a finite triangle-free graph \(H\).
453	
454	Choose even \(k\) so large that, writing \(p=p_k\),
455	\[
456	\frac{p}{3(1+p)}>c. \tag{12}
457	\]
458	Choose \(m\) with
459	\[
460	\chi(F)>|V(H)|,\qquad F=S(m,k).
461	\]
462	
463	Replace every edge \(uv\) of \(F\) by a path
464	\[
465	x_u-y_{uv}-z_{uv}-x_v,
466	\]
467	choosing an arbitrary orientation \(u\to v\) for each edge. Call the resulting graph \(Q\), with its three independent classes \(Q_0,Q_1,Q_2\) of original, first internal, and second internal vertices.
468	
469	Define a homomorphism \(\ell:Q\to F\) by
470	\[
471	\ell(x_u)=u,\qquad \ell(y_{uv})=v,\qquad \ell(z_{uv})=u.
472	\]
473	
474	Choose a positive integer \(M\), and put \(N=M2^m\). For each \(i=0,1,2\):
475	
476	* add an independent set \(U_i\), consisting of \(M\) copies of every sign vector \(\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^m\);
477	* add an independent set \(V_i\) of size \(pN\);
478	* join \(U_i\) completely to \(V_i\);
479	* join \(q\in Q_i\) to the copies of \(\epsilon\) precisely when
480	  \[
481	  h_\epsilon(\ell(q))>3.
482	  \]
483	
484	There are no other edges. Since \(m\ge k\), \(pN\) is an integer.
485	
486	Call the graph \(G\). Every vertex of \(Q\) gets exactly \(pN\) neighbors in its corresponding \(U_i\). Every vertex of \(U_i\) has \(pN\) neighbors in \(V_i\), and every vertex of \(V_i\) has \(N\) neighbors. Hence
487	\[
488	\delta(G)\ge pN,\qquad
489	|V(G)|=|V(Q)|+3(1+p)N. \tag{13}
490	\]
491	By (12), sufficiently large \(M\) makes
492	\[
493	\delta(G)\ge c|V(G)|.
494	\]
495	
496	### There are no triangles or five-cycles
497	
498	The graph \(Q\) itself has no cycle of length less than \(9\).
499	
500	A triangle or five-cycle cannot contain a vertex of \(V_i\). For a five-cycle through such a vertex, the remaining three-edge path between its two neighbors in \(U_i\) would require an edge inside \(Q_i\cup V_i\), but this set is independent.
501	
502	Now consider a short odd cycle avoiding all \(V_i\).
503	
504	* A triangle using \(U_i\) would require an edge within \(Q_i\).
505	* A five-cycle using exactly one vertex of some \(U_i\) gives a three-edge path in \(Q\) between two of its neighbors. Applying \(\ell\) and (10), their scores cannot both exceed \(3\).
506	* A five-cycle using two vertices from the \(U_i\)'s has the form
507	  \[
508	  u-q-u'-q'-q''-u.
509	  \]
510	  The common neighbor \(q\) forces \(u,u'\) to belong to the same \(U_i\). Then \(q',q''\in Q_i\), contradicting their adjacency.
511	
512	Thus \(G\) contains neither \(C_3\) nor \(C_5\).
513	
514	### There is no homomorphism \(G\to H\)
515	
516	Suppose \(f:G\to H\). For each edge \(uv\in E(F)\), its replacing three-edge path in \(Q\) shows that
517	\[
518	f(x_u)\ne f(x_v),
519	\]
520	because otherwise its image is a closed three-edge walk in the triangle-free graph \(H\).
521	
522	Therefore \(u\mapsto f(x_u)\) is a proper coloring of \(F\) with at most \(|V(H)|\) colors, contradicting the choice of \(F\).
523	
524	This constructs, for every finite triangle-free \(H\), a counterexample of minimum-degree ratio at least \(c\). Hence no \(c<1/9\) has the required property.

528	# 4. Proof of the regularity ingredient
529	
530	Here are the details needed to make the upper bound independent of an unproved regularity theorem.
531	
532	For disjoint nonempty sets \(A,B\), write
533	\[
534	d(A,B)=\frac{e(A,B)}{|A||B|}.
535	\]
536	The pair is \(\varepsilon\)-regular if every \(A'\subseteq A,B'\subseteq B\) with
537	\[
538	|A'|\ge\varepsilon|A|,\qquad |B'|\ge\varepsilon|B|
539	\]
540	satisfies
541	\[
542	|d(A',B')-d(A,B)|\le\varepsilon.
543	\]
544	
545	We prove that, for fixed \(\varepsilon>0,k_0\), sufficiently large graphs have an equitable partition into boundedly many clusters, an exceptional set of size at most \(\varepsilon n\), and at most \(\varepsilon k^2\) irregular cluster pairs.
546	
547	For a partition \(\mathcal P\), define its energy by
548	\[
549	\mathcal E(\mathcal P)
550	=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{A,B\in\mathcal P}|A||B|d(A,B)^2,
551	\]
552	using ordered adjacency densities also when \(A=B\). It lies in \([0,1]\), and refinement cannot decrease it, by the weighted mean-square inequality.
553	
554	Start with \(k_0\) equal clusters and fewer than \(k_0\) exceptional vertices, treating exceptional vertices as singleton parts for energy calculations.
555	
556	Suppose there are more than \(\varepsilon k^2\) irregular pairs among equal clusters of size \(m\). Choose a witnessing rectangle for each irregular pair and refine every cluster by all its witnessing subsets. There are at most \(2^k\) resulting cells per cluster.
557	
558	For each irregular ordered block, the energy increases by at least
559	\[
560	\frac{m^2}{n^2}\varepsilon^4:
561	\]
562	the witness has relative area at least \(\varepsilon^2\), and its density differs by more than \(\varepsilon\). Accounting for both orders, the total increase exceeds
563	\[
564	2\varepsilon^5\left(\frac{km}{n}\right)^2.
565	\]
566	While the exceptional set has size at most \(n/2\), this is at least \(\varepsilon^5/2\).
567	
568	It remains to keep the clusters equal without losing control of the exception. Put
569	\[
570	s=\left\lceil4\varepsilon^{-5}\right\rceil,\qquad
571	B(k)=\left\lceil\frac{4s\,2^k}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil.
572	\]
573	After the witness refinement, subdivide every cell into pieces of common size
574	\[
575	q=\left\lfloor\frac{m}{B(k)}\right\rfloor
576	\]
577	and put its remainder into the exceptional set as singletons. This is still a refinement, so energy does not decrease. The number of newly exceptional vertices is at most
578	\[
579	k2^kq\le\frac{\varepsilon n}{4s}.
580	\]
581	Provided \(m\ge2B(k)\), the new number of clusters is at most \(4kB(k)\).
582	
583	Starting from \(k_0\), iterating the finite bound
584	\[
585	K\longmapsto4KB(K)
586	\]
587	for \(s\) steps bounds every cluster count by a finite constant \(K_*\). Taking \(n\) sufficiently large ensures \(m\ge2B(K_*)\), and makes the initial exception at most \(\varepsilon n/4\).
588	
589	There can be fewer than \(s\) energy-increasing rounds, since energy is at most \(1\). The total exception remains below \(\varepsilon n\). Therefore the process terminates with the required regular partition. Increasing the threshold on \(n\) makes the final cluster size exceed any prescribed constant.
590	
591	Finally, the short-path facts used in Section 2 follow directly from regularity: for a subset \(A\) of one side of size at least \(\varepsilon m\), fewer than \(\varepsilon m\) vertices on the other side have fewer than
592	\[
593	(d-\varepsilon)|A|
594	\]
595	neighbors in \(A\). Apply this to one or two prescribed subsets. With the parameters in Section 2 and sufficiently large clusters, the paths can avoid any three prescribed vertices.
596	
597	This completes the regularity argument used above.
